Today's big story: Anthropic Below Its IPO Price: Do Giants Come Back?

Palantir Technologies has the highest price for its profit in its group of five large technology companies.
Its shares trade at 105.7 times its past year's profit, the top figure in the group. It also has the fastest sales growth, 87.1% in the four quarters to September 30, 2026. So are you overpaying, or paying for growth no rival in the group delivers?

We looked at this group on Tuesday. For that piece, see Is Palantir Stock Priced Right Against Its Rivals? This one asks what the extra price pays for.

How much more does Palantir cost than its rivals?

The price-to-earnings ratio, or P/E, is the share price divided by a year's profit per share. A higher P/E means you pay more for each dollar the company earns.

Microsoft makes the sharpest contrast. Its P/E is 25.8. It keeps a slightly larger share of sales as operating profit, 47.1% against Palantir's 45.6%. That share is the operating margin. But Microsoft grew sales 17.9%, far below Palantir's 87.1%.

Palantir pays no dividend. So everything a holder earns has to come from the share price, which closed at $161.18 on Tuesday.

Palantir sends its owners no cash, so at $161 a share any gain must come from the price rising. If you need your savings to cover the bills each month, this stock will not send you a check while you hold it.. The Trefis Income Solution pays a dividend yield about 3 times the S&P 500's, from 50 companies that have paid dividends for at least 10 years in a row. See what it pays.

Every other peer sits below Palantir on both price and growth. So the highest P/E comes with the highest growth. On margin, Palantir ranks second of five.

One caution applies to the P/E. Palantir's net income of $3.67 billion was above its operating income of $3.33 billion. So income outside the main business lifted the profit behind its P/E. Alphabet and Amazon show the same pattern. The businesses differ too. Amazon is classed as a broadline retailer, and International Business Machines sells IT services.

What does the extra price pay for?

Growth sped up in the latest quarter. Revenue in the three months to September 2026 rose 95.9% from a year earlier, up from 92.8% in the quarter before. Management said it was the first quarter in which U.S. commercial revenue was larger than U.S. government revenue.

Profit grew faster than sales. The operating margin was 13.8% in the four quarters to September 2024. It rose to 21.8% a year later and to 45.6% now. That is the highest of the 26 quarter ends in the data, which start in mid-2020.

What number would settle it?

Management expects revenue of $8.53 billion for fiscal 2026, the year ending December 2026. That would be growth of 91%. For the three months to December, it expects $2.65 billion, against $1.41 billion a year earlier. That would be growth of about 88%, below the 95.9% of the September quarter. The next report, due in February, 2027, will show whether December-quarter revenue reached $2.65 billion.

The risk is that a price this high leaves little room for a slower quarter. The stock fell 18.9% in the month to November 24, while the S&P 500 lost 6.1%, both counting dividends. Rivals compare on cash flow and sales in the peer valuation table for Palantir.

What does the price ask Palantir to keep doing?

Our read: Palantir's top P/E in this group comes with the group's fastest growth, so you are not paying for nothing. The price asks Palantir to keep growing far faster than its four rivals, with its margin at its highest in our data. So far the evidence supports both: growth sped up in the September quarter, and the four-quarter margin kept rising. But management's guide for the December quarter points to slower growth.

Still, all of that rests on one company keeping a pace none of its rivals match. Spreading your money across many strong businesses means no single report decides how you do.

title: 'Big Short' Investor Michael Burry Just Closed His Bet Against the Nasdaq. Here's What Investors Should Do Now
detail:
'Big Short' Investor Michael Burry Just Closed His Bet Against the Nasdaq. Here's What Investors Should Do Now
Jonathan Ponciano, The Motley Fool
Wed, November 25, 2026 at 5:20 PM CST 4 min read
NVDA
^IXIC
PLTR
MET
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Michael Burry made his name betting against the housing market before the 2008 financial crisis. This week, with tech stocks in a steep slide, he did something somewhat unusual for him: He stopped betting against the market.

In a post on his Substack, Cassandra Unchained, Burry said he had sold the rest of his put options on the Nasdaq-100, bearish bets that pay off when the index falls. "Globally, my portfolio is more long, and less short, than it has been in some time," he wrote. Apart from puts on Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ:PLTR) and MetLife (NYSE:MET), he added, "I am temporarily almost entirely long."

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Michael Burry. Image source: Getty Images.

Why the Timing Matters

Burry is turning more bullish after a sharp drop. The Nasdaq Composite closed Tuesday at 23,733.54, down 14.5% from its Oct. 6 close, and the Nasdaq-100 fell 16% over the same stretch. The Composite is down about 7% in November alone, as doubts about whether the AI spending boom will pay off, new tariff proposals, and the turmoil around Nvidia's leadership have weighed on AI stocks.

Puts gain value as an index falls, so selling them after a slide is a way to lock in profits. Burry said much of his cash, about 25% of the portfolio, came from profitable put options plus money added to the account.

He Isn't Calling a Bottom

The most important word in his post may be "temporarily." Burry said he is "continuing to assess short opportunities," and he hasn't said the market has bottomed. He also kept his Palantir puts, even though Palantir shares, at about $164 on Wednesday, already sit roughly 23% below their 52-week high.

Burry disclosed large put positions on Nvidia and Palantir in late 2025 after warning about an AI bubble. Shifting from that stance to mostly long tells you he thinks a good part of the downside he expected has now played out, at least for the broad index.

What Investors Should Do Now

For most investors, the answer is not to copy his trades. Burry can reverse a position in a day and write about it afterward, so by the time a move becomes news, he may have changed it again. Short-selling and options are tools most individual investors shouldn't rely on.

The useful lesson is in how he's behaving. He took profits on a bet that worked, he's holding a big cash cushion, and he's staying selective about what he owns. You can do a version of that: Make a list of quality tech stocks you'd be glad to own for five years, and buy them in stages if the sell-off continues, rather than all at once. Keep enough cash on the side that you're never forced to sell in a downturn.

title: Goldman Sachs bets on Palantir's 'mega customers' after NYC demo
detail:
Goldman Sachs bets on Palantir's 'mega customers' after NYC demo
Opeyemi Babalola, Celine Provini
Wed, November 25, 2026 at 2:13 PM CST 5 min read
PLTR
Trade PLTR on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Most of us have sat through a software demo that dazzled on the big screen and fell apart on our own laptop.

Goldman Sachs analysts got a different kind of show when they visited Palantir Technologies (PLTR) in New York on Nov. 18. They walked out with evidence of what happens long after the sales pitch ends.

The session with CFO Dave Glazer and Chief Architect Akshay Krishnaswamy shaped a Goldman note shared with TheStreet, dated Nov. 22.

Also read: Palantir's revenue nearly doubled as contract growth slowed

Analyst Gabriela Borges kept a Buy rating and a $235 price target. That conviction stands out because Palantir shares have spent weeks heading the other way.

Small pilots are turning into eight-figure contracts

The most telling detail is what customers do after they sign. Palantir customers often expand roughly 18 months into a deployment, according to Goldman. Disclosed examples have grown five to 15 times in annual contract value, the analysts wrote.

The individual cases are hard to ignore. A global athletic company grew from $1.6 million to about $21 million, Goldman said. A home appliance maker jumped from $1 million to $15 million, according to the note. An apparel company climbed from $2.5 million to $11.5 million, the analysts added.

Growth like that turns ordinary accounts into mega customers. Average U.S. commercial revenue per customer now sits near $5 million, Goldman estimated. Newer customers are scaling faster than earlier ones.

The quiet advantage is cost. Palantir already has access to each client's data, business rules and ontology, its digital map of how a company runs. Goldman argued that gives each added workflow attractive economics.

Goldman Sachs says recent Palantir pilots grew five to 15 times in contract value, with one athletic brand rising from $1.6 million to about $21 million.hapabapa / Getty Images
Palantir's lean model keeps the expansion repeatable

Expansion only scales if Palantir does not need an army to deliver it. Goldman described Palantir as an operating layer that sits across rival AI models and data platforms such as Databricks and Snowflake (SNOW).

Management also said more data now flows out of Palantir's systems than into them, as decisions feed back into daily operations.

People still matter. Palantir's forward deployed engineers build around a customer's problem, working "backward from the outcome," as Goldman put it. Foundry, its core platform, has grown from four microservices to more than 300, the note said, so work that once took months now takes days.

Customers are also doing more of the building. Airbus (EADSY), a longtime client, supports about 12,000 technical users on the platform, according to Goldman.

Michael Burry, the investor who famously predicted the 2008 housing market crash, is now betting on a stock market recovery.

On Wednesday, he revealed that he had closed his remaining bets against the Nasdaq 100, as the tech-heavy index briefly fell 20% from its October record high.

What Is Michael Burry Predicting Now?

In a Substack post, Burry revealed that he had taken profits from his bets on falling stock prices. Almost all his remaining investments are now positioned to benefit from rising prices.

He is still betting against two companies: Palantir and MetLife.

Michael Burry Stock Market Prediction

Around 25% of his portfolio remains in cash, which he is gradually looking to invest.

However, Burry made it clear that his bullish outlook is temporary.

"Right now apart from Palantir puts and MetLife puts, I am temporarily almost entirely long. Temporarily, because I am continuing to assess short opportunities."

His latest moves suggest he sees buying opportunities following the recent market crash. However, he has made no explicit prediction that the stock market has bottomed or that a sustained recovery is coming.

Days earlier, Burry also sold half of his bets against Nvidia before the chipmaker's shares rallied.

Why Are Stocks Falling the Day Before Thanksgiving?

The Trump administration proposed new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China, the European Union, Japan, and India. Chinese goods face up to 20% on top of roughly 25% in existing duties.

Inflation added to the pressure. The PCE index, the Federal Reserve's preferred price gauge, rose 3.8% from a year earlier in October.

Traders now price a 97% chance of a Fed rate hike in December.

By 10 a.m. ET, the Nasdaq Composite was down about 4% and the S&P 500 about 2.7%.

Nasdaq Composite and S&P 500 Performance. Source: TradingView

Nvidia fell 8% to roughly $141, with the move erasing more than half of Monday's 31% jump, which followed Jensen Huang's reinstatement as CEO.

Nvidia has lost $2 trillion in market value from its October peak.

Other chipmakers fared worse. SanDisk dropped 12% and Micron about 10%, while Ambarella plunged 25% after a weak forecast.

Together, the US stock market had wiped out over $1.7 trillion at market open.

The slide also breaks a holiday pattern. Since 1950, the S&P 500 has risen on the Wednesday before Thanksgiving in 58 of 76 years, Motley Fool data shows.

Investor Jeremy Lefebvre flagged the break from that pattern on X.

"The stock market almost NEVER crashes or even goes down the day before Thanksgiving. The fact this is occurring is a BAD OMEN. Even in 2018 the Nasdaq found a way to go up .9%," noted investor Jeremy Lefebvre.

Burry's exit from index shorts comes after he warned about AI stocks for weeks.

However, the next tests sit beyond the holiday. Comments on the tariff plan are due Jan. 5, with hearings starting Jan. 25.

title: Peter Thiel Buys $122M of PLTR After Years Of Selling — And He Could Buy Millions More Shares

Daragh Thomas

Billionaire investor Peter Thiel has sold nearly $2.6 billion worth of Palantir Technologies Inc. (NASDAQ:PLTR) stock since the company went public in 2020, but now he's buying.

An SEC filing Tuesday night revealed that Palantir's co-founder and chairman bought $122.3 million worth of shares on Friday at an average price of $143.81, after the stock had fallen more than 30% from its October high.

It was his first reported open-market purchase since Palantir went public, and he paid almost exactly the same price at which he sold $290 million worth of shares in March.

Same Price, Different Palantir

Palantir's business has grown considerably in the intervening eight months. The company's quarterly revenue increased 64% between its February and November earnings reports, from $1.41 billion to $2.31 billion.

But investors have reason to worry about whether Palantir can sustain that growth. The value of new contracts the company signed in its latest quarter grew just 6% year over year, with analysts at William Blair flagging slowing U.S. commercial bookings as a concern.

Thiel's 90-Day Wait

Thiel's return to buying Palantir stock had been months in the making. On Aug. 19, he established a trading plan that would allow him to buy up to four million shares through December 2027.

Under SEC rules, company directors must wait at least 90 days before they can trade under such plans. Thiel reached that threshold on November 17, but made no reported purchases while Palantir traded above $153 over the next three sessions.

When the stock plunged 6.6% on Friday, Thiel bought 850,100 shares at prices ranging from $142.29 to $144.85. The highest price he paid matched, to the cent, the average price at which he sold in March.

That suggests Thiel may have set up his plan to buy shares only at or below his March selling price.

Will Investors Get Thiel's Price?

Palantir rebounded more than 12% over the next two trading sessions, and Cathie Wood's Ark Invest used the rally to sell $7.2 million worth of shares on Tuesday. But the stock was falling again Wednesday amid a broader sell-off.

Whether Palantir gets back to Thiel's price may depend on the wider AI trade. Traders on Polymarket put the odds of the AI bubble bursting by the end of 2026 at 34%, rising to 56% by the middle of next year.

Thiel's trading plan still leaves room for another 3.15 million shares, but the price at which Palantir's chairman might buy again remains undisclosed.

Snowflake shows a milder version of the same gap. Its product revenue grew 37% to $1.49 billion in its quarter ended July 31, while its remaining performance obligations grew 30% to $9.00 billion. title: Palantir Is Down 25% From Its High. Is It a Bargain or Still Overvalued?
detail:
Palantir Is Down 25% From Its High. Is It a Bargain or Still Overvalued?
Micah Zimmerman, The Motley Fool
Wed, November 25, 2026 at 11:20 AM CST 5 min read
PLTR
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

There's a sentence in Palantir Technologies' (NASDAQ:PLTR) quarterly filing that most investors skim right past: The company says it "allows many of its customers to terminate contracts for convenience prior to the end of the stated term with less than 12 months' notice."

That fine print matters more now that the stock has cooled. Shares recently closed at $159, about 25% below their all-time intraday high of $212.94. Part of the pressure came from the third quarter, when total contract value signed grew just 6%.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Is it a bargain? Not by the usual yardsticks. At 112 times trailing earnings, the price-to-earnings ratio assumes years of fast growth. But I think the market misreads Palantir's government business, starting with that clause.

The backlog that leaves out the Pentagon

Palantir's backlog, $4.9 billion in remaining performance obligations (RPO), was flat from the prior quarter. CFO David Glazer explained during the earnings call why that's only half the story:

RPO is primarily comprised of our commercial business as it does not take into account contracts with an initial term of less than 12 months and contractual obligations that fall beyond termination for convenience clauses, both of which are common in most of our government business.

The filing adds that "the U.S. federal government is prohibited from exercising contract options more than one year in advance." So the backlog largely excludes Uncle Sam, even as government revenue grew 81% to $1.15 billion in the third quarter.

On the ground, it works like a tab. In 2025, the Army folded 75 Palantir contracts into one enterprise agreement worth up to $10 billion over 10 years, stressing that the cap "represents the maximum potential value of the contract, not any specific obligations or commitments." One Maven Smart System order under that agreement has been funded in eight separate steps since November 2025, reaching about $637 million. Even the Navy buys Palantir licenses through it.

Image source: The Motley Fool.

Cancelable on paper, sticky in practice

A contract you can cancel on short notice sounds fragile, but what matters is whether customers leave. What I like so much about this ticker is the kind of customers Palantir has and the amount of money they represent. France's domestic intelligence agency renewed for three more years in December 2025. "This contract renewal reaffirms Palantir's commitment to serving the interests of France since 2016," CEO Alex Karp said.

Investing.com -- Michael Burry, the investor who famously bet against the U.S. housing market ahead of the 2008 financial crisis, has sold the remainder of his bearish Nasdaq 100 position, saying his portfolio is now temporarily almost entirely long amid heightened market volatility.

Burry said he exited the final half of his Nasdaq 100 (NDX) put position on Wednesday as technology stocks came under renewed pressure, according to comments shared with subscribers and reported by Bloomberg.

The move represents a notable shift in positioning for the investor, who has become widely known for his bearish market calls and willingness to take concentrated positions against prevailing trends.

"Globally, my portfolio is more long, and less short, than it has been in some time," Burry told subscribers.

He said that, aside from put positions on Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ: PLTR) and MetLife (NYSE: MET), his portfolio was temporarily almost entirely long.

"Temporarily, because I am continuing to assess short opportunities," he added.

Burry also disclosed that he was holding approximately 25% of his portfolio in cash and was looking for opportunities to deploy the capital. He said the cash came largely from successful put positions, along with additional money added to the accounts.

"If I cannot, so it is," he said, indicating that he was not prepared to force investments simply to put the available cash to work.

The investor also outlined his approach to position sizing, dividing holdings into three categories: larger positions representing 8% to 20% or more of a portfolio, normal positions accounting for 3% to 6%, and smaller positions typically representing 2% to 3% or less.

Burry's decision to close his remaining Nasdaq 100 puts is particularly notable given the recent pressure on technology stocks and broader concerns surrounding the cost of the artificial intelligence infrastructure buildout.

However, his comments do not necessarily signal that he believes the market has reached a bottom or that he has abandoned his bearish outlook. He explicitly described his predominantly long positioning as temporary and said he was continuing to evaluate potential short opportunities.

For now, the message is that one of Wall Street's best-known bears has substantially reduced his bearish exposure, while retaining a sizable cash position and the flexibility to change direction.

title: Palantir’s CEO Alex Karp Sold $75 Million. Co-Founder Peter Thiel Bought $122 Million
detail:
Palantir’s CEO Alex Karp Sold $75 Million. Co-Founder Peter Thiel Bought $122 Million
Omor Ibne Ehsan
Wed, November 25, 2026 at 7:53 AM CST 5 min read
PLTR
Trade PLTR on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Quick Read

Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel bought $122 million of stock while CEO Alex Karp sold $75 million, but preset rules drove most of both trades.

Thiel's plan bought on a 7% selloff near the day's low, and his average price sat below his March sale price.

Palantir trades at 229 times earnings while contract value grew just 6%, leaving little room for error despite revenue nearly doubling.

Read: Building a portfolio and living off one are two completely different skills, and almost nobody teaches the second. This problem is what The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income helps with, and it is free today. Read more here.

Two well-known insiders traded in opposite directions on the same Friday, and their Form 4s were filed together after the close on Tuesday evening, November 24.

Neilson Barnard / Getty Images for New York Times

Co-founder and director Peter Thiel bought 850,100 Class A shares of Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ:PLTR) on November 20 for about $122.3 million. CEO Alex Karp sold 493,263 shares across November 20 and 23 for about $75.1 million.

The numbers support the headline contrast, but preset rules force most of both trades. Thiel's purchases ran under a Rule 10b5-1 plan he adopted on August 19, 2026. About 82% of Karp's proceeds went to cover tax withholding on vested restricted stock units. Wednesday is the first session where the market can react to both filings.

Thiel's Plan Bought on the Selloff Day

Thiel's plan bought on a day when Palantir fell 6.63% to close at $143.49. His fills ran from $142.29 to $144.85, close to the $142.28 intraday low, and averaged about $143.81.

The shares are held by PLTR Holdings II LLC, which Thiel holds alone. The Form 4 lists 69,721,656 Class A shares in total, and the filing itself says that count is incomplete.

The plan set the timing in August. Putting more than $122 million of his own money to work at these prices was still Thiel's decision.

------

Many successful investors eventually reach the same moment. The saving is done, the portfolio is built, and the question quietly changes from how much can I grow this to how much can I take out? Get that second question wrong and decades of good investing can come apart in a handful of years.

That is exactly what The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income helps answer. It covers what your retirement could actually cost, which income sources are worth using, and the withdrawal math that decides whether the money lasts. It is free today from Fisher Investments. Read More Here ›

------

He Bought Back Below His March Sale Price

His previous Form 4 showed him selling 2,000,000 shares on March 2, 2026, at about $144.85 on average. That sale ran under a plan he adopted on November 14, 2025. His November buys came in below that average, so he did not pay up after a rally.

At Tuesday's $161.18 close, the new shares showed a paper gain of about $14.8 million, or about 12%. The shares listed on the filing were worth about $11.2 billion.

Karp's Sales Followed a Tax Schedule

Karp had 975,000 Class B restricted stock units vest on November 20. To cover withholding, he sold 163,319 shares that day and 239,944 on November 23, worth about $61.9 million combined. That was about 181,700 fewer tax shares than his Form 144 notices covered.

He also sold 90,000 shares for about $13.20 million under a plan he entered on March 12, 2026, and he gave 58,562 shares to public charities. He still holds 6,432,258 Class A and 52,916,076 Class B shares directly, plus unvested units.

Rebound Leaves Palantir's Valuation Stretched

Palantir rose 11.06% on Monday and 1.14% on Tuesday, for a $388.36 billion market value. At 7:59 p.m. ET Tuesday, it was quoted after hours at $160.05.

The stock is still down 18.08% over the past month and 9.32% year to date. Even so, it trades at 229 times earnings and 177 times free cash flow.

Third-quarter revenue rose 95.87% to $2.313 billion. Total contract value grew just 6%, though, and stock-based compensation rose to $318.9 million from $172.3 million a year earlier.

PCE inflation, GDP, durable goods and jobless claims are due at 8:30 a.m. ET Wednesday, and markets close Thursday for Thanksgiving.

PLTR Price Target — 24/7 Wall St.
Should You Buy or Sell PLTR Stock

Long-term investors exploring Palantir may want to consider the insider activity against the stock's valuation and volatility. A founder putting more than $122 million of his own money into the stock is a rarer signal than an executive's routine tax sales.

Tuesday's close sat about 12% above Thiel's average price, for a stock that swung 6.63% and 11.06% on back-to-back sessions. Swings that big make the stock's entry price hard to judge.

U.S. commercial revenue of $984 million passed government revenue for the first time, and the company expects $4.8 billion to $5.0 billion of adjusted free cash flow this year. If bookings keep growing near 6%, the valuation leaves little room for error, so position sizing is a key consideration for anyone exploring the stock.
